presentingComplaint: Sudden onset of large-volume vomiting of fresh blood, followed by two episodes of black tarry stool over the preceding 12 hours.
history: Known cirrhotic (chronic hepatitis B related, Child-Pugh B) with a history of alcohol excess, previously found on surveillance endoscopy to have grade II esophageal varices not on primary prophylaxis. Presents with sudden-onset hematemesis (approximately 400 mL of fresh blood) at home, followed by one episode of melena. Reports feeling dizzy and light-headed on standing, with one brief syncopal episode just before arrival. No prior variceal bleed. No NSAID or antiplatelet use. No fever or abdominal pain preceding the bleed. Family noted increasing abdominal girth over the past month and mild confusion over the last day.
examination: Pale, diaphoretic, mildly disoriented (oriented to person only) male in mild distress. Stigmata of chronic liver disease: palmar erythema, spider angiomata over chest, scleral icterus. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness consistent with ascites; no localized tenderness; liver not palpable, spleen tip palpable. Mild asterixis present. Digital rectal exam confirms melena. Cool peripheries with delayed capillary refill.
imaging: Prior upper GI endoscopy (surveillance): grade II esophageal varices without red wale signs, not on primary prophylaxis
Abdominal ultrasound: cirrhotic liver contour, splenomegaly, moderate ascites, patent portal vein on this admission
microbiology: Diagnostic ascitic tap sent for cell count and culture to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) as bleed precipitant
finalDiagnosis: Acute variceal hemorrhage (esophageal varices) in decompensated cirrhosis
citations: AASLD Practice Guidance — Portal Hypertensive Bleeding in Cirrhosis 2017
stewardship: Short-course prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) recommended in all cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding per AASLD/Baveno VII, regardless of overt infection, to reduce rebleeding and mortality risk from SBP/bacterial translocation
contraindications: Avoid vasopressin alone (use terlipressin/octreotide instead) due to systemic vasoconstriction risk
Avoid over-transfusion beyond restrictive target (Hb ~7-8 g/dL) as it can worsen portal pressure and rebleeding
Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic agents in decompensated cirrhosis
Caution with sedation for endoscopy given hepatic encephalopathy and risk of aspiration
edgeCases: Concurrent hepatic encephalopathy (asterixis, disorientation) may mask or mimic hypovolemic shock-related confusion
Coagulopathy (INR 1.9, platelets 78) reflects synthetic dysfunction, not primarily consumptive; correction strategy differs from DIC
Must exclude SBP as a precipitant of bleed via diagnostic paracentesis

If bleeding source were instead a bleeding peptic ulcer in a cirrhotic (portal hypertensive patient), management diverges significantly (PPI-based vs vasoactive-drug based) — this case is written specifically as variceal etiology
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag this as a high-severity variceal hemorrhage in decompensated cirrhosis, recommend urgent resuscitation with restrictive transfusion strategy, vasoactive drug therapy (terlipressin/octreotide) plus prophylactic antibiotics, and emergent endoscopy with band ligation within 12 hours; should also surface hepatic encephalopathy and coagulopathy as complicating factors.

Any recent alcohol intake or medication non-adherence (e.g., non-selective beta-blocker)?
Is the patient a transplant candidate (relevant to overall management ceiling)?
